title: Flights diverted after Manchester Airport security breach
author: Angela Ferguson
content:
![An airplane is on the runway, with grass in the foreground and an airport in the background with Manchester emblazoned on it](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/9a6e/live/f3c08310-9dfe-11f1-a114-3124d9d4dc72.jpg)
Seven flights had to be diverted while others circled over Manchester Airport
- Published
Seven flights had to be diverted and 17 held in the skies above Manchester Airport after a man trespassed on the airfield.
It happened at about 23:21 BST on Friday and the airfield had to be closed for 15 minutes, while police attended and arrested the man.
Greater Manchester Police said: "We responded to reports of male who had been located air-side at Manchester Airport.
"This appears to be mental-health related and the man has been taken to hospital for assessment."
Part of an airfield fence, which was damaged, has been fixed, the airport added.
Listen to the best of BBC Radio Manchester on Sounds and follow BBC Manchester on Facebook, external, X, external, and Instagram, external. You can also send story ideas via Whatsapp to 0808 100 2230.
summary: Manchester Airport experienced a 15-minute airfield closure after a man trespassed into the air-side area on Friday night. The incident resulted in seven diverted flights and 17 aircraft holding in the skies above. Police arrested the man, who was subsequently taken to the hospital for a mental health assessment.
key_points: A man trespassed air-side at Manchester Airport at about 23:21 BST on Friday.
The airfield was closed for 15 minutes while police responded and arrested the individual.
Seven flights were diverted and 17 were held in the air during the incident.
Police stated the incident was mental-health related and the man was taken to hospital for assessment.
Airport staff repaired a damaged section of the airfield fence following the breach.

title: Laptop catches fire on US flight, with passenger treated at airport
author: Mallory Moench
content:
![The front of an air plane with the American logo on a runway.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1024/cpsprodpb/c85e/live/8f3dc3c0-9e09-11f1-95e0-53a570c83624.jpg)
American Airlines Flight 2398, an Airbus A321 like the plane pictured here, landed safely at Dallas Forth Worth airport
- Published
One person has received medical treatment after a passenger's laptop caught fire on an American Airlines flight.
The pilot had reported a "cabin fire in the back of the airplane" to air traffic control, saying "the flight attendants are trying to put it out now", according to audio obtained by the BBC's US reporting partner CBS News.
"I think we have about four to five passengers that were burned by the laptop. The laptop is contained about mid-aircraft."
One passenger received medical attention on site and was released after American Airlines Flight 2398 - coming from Atlanta, Georgia - landed at Dallas Fort Worth International Airport in Texas on Friday.
The airline told the BBC that the flight landed safely "after reports of smoke from a customer's device during landing. We thank our crew for their professionalism and swift response to quickly contain the device."
After landing, the aircraft taxied to the gate, and emergency personnel met the aircraft upon arrival, per procedure.
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) warns that lithium batteries, including laptop batteries, are capable of overheating, external "as a result of various factors, including if the battery is damaged, overheated, exposed to water, overcharged, or improperly packed".
The FAA recorded , external58 verified lithium battery air incidents so far this year involving smoke, fire or extreme heat. In the last 20 years, the highest number of incidents was related to battery packs, with 84 cases related to laptops.
Lithium batteries must be stowed in carry-on baggage only, the US regulator says.
In May, a UK-bound EasyJet flight from Egypt was diverted to Rome after a power bank was found to be charging in a passenger's luggage in the hold of the aircraft. The flight was rescheduled for the next day.
The UK's aviation regulator the Civil Aviation Authority has said power banks are causing a growing number of serious issues on flights worldwide, and urged more awareness as portable chargers carry "serious risks" of overheating or catching fire.
summary: One person received medical treatment after a passenger's laptop caught fire aboard an American Airlines flight traveling from Atlanta to Dallas. The flight landed safely, and the crew quickly contained the device before emergency personnel met the aircraft at the gate. The FAA notes that lithium batteries, including those in laptops, carry risks of overheating and have been involved in dozens of air incidents this year.
key_points: A laptop caught fire on American Airlines Flight 2398.
One passenger was treated at the airport and released.
The aircraft landed safely at Dallas Fort Worth International Airport.
The FAA has recorded 58 verified lithium battery air incidents this year involving smoke, fire, or extreme heat.
Lithium batteries must be stowed in carry-on baggage only according to US regulators.

title: Plug-in solar: could a low-cost panel cut your bills?
author: Zoe Wood
content:
Despite this summer bringing hours of sunshine, many Britons have been unable to cash in on free electricity generated by the sun. Rooftop solar panels are usually out of the question if you live in a flat or rent your home, and the cost has made them prohibitive to many more households.
However, this could be about to change because next week the first wave of low-cost “plug-in” solar panels will go on sale in Great Britain.
Also known as “plug‑and‑play” or “balcony” solar, the clue to what makes them different is in the name: you can fix them to a balcony or garden wall, then plug them in like a toaster.
The mini solar systems are a familiar sight on balconies in Spain and in Germany, where they are known as a Balkonkraftwerk (balcony power plant), but until a recent change in the law, they were not permitted in Britain.
Matt Parry from the Renewable Energy Association, a trade body for renewable energy, says the kits are a gamechanger. “It democratises solar and gives everyone the chance to get it,” he says.
How the kits work
Unlike traditional rooftop solar panels, which require a professional to install, balcony solar kits – which commonly include one or two panels – can be plugged in to a three-prong wall socket.
You can fix them on a balcony railing, shed roof or garden wall – anywhere with good sun exposure and safe access.
When sunlight hits the solar panels, they generate a direct current. The microinverter then converts this to an alternating current, which flows into your home’s electrical system, reducing the amount you draw from the grid.
![A balcony power station on the balcony railings of a home](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/a3c7aa28a0d3eb66717231c4b2fce69f8f8f691c/863_48_7393_5456/master/7393.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Previously, rules around the installation of solar were what was holding people back. But last year the government announced it would make it possible for plug-in solar to be used in this country.
To make this a reality, it has updated wiring regulations to allow households in Great Britain to connect plug-in solar panels capable of generating up to 800 watts of power into the mains without the need for an electrician. (The rules are different in Northern Ireland.)
Buying panels
Big names including B&Q, Currys, Lidl, Wickes and Amazon are lining up to sell plug-in solar.
Given the size (and weight) of these devices, it is expected that many will be bought online.
![A person carries a television outside a Currys store in London](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/829a8168fddef51acb05cae7243f22cb66d62fb0/873_0_5000_4000/master/5000.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Although you may have already come across plug-in solar panels for sale, industry experts suggest waiting until the regulations take effect on 27 August before making a purchase.
Electrical Safety First, the consumer safety charity, is urging shoppers to stick to reputable high street retailers and their websites to ensure the device complies with the rules.
Luke Osborne, the charity’s technical director, advises people to “avoid buying these devices from third-party sellers on online marketplaces. These platforms are now not legally responsible for the safety of goods sold via their sites, exposing people to substandard versions that may put you and your home at risk.”
Andrew Moore, the founder of the British solar panel brand UKSOL, says: “We are working towards making the initial products available from 27 August.”
His company will initially sell 460W and 890W kits, starting at £599 and £999 respectively, and it plans to launch another four models in late September, with prices starting from £499.
Sizewise, plug-in solar setups are usually smaller than rooftop options, but sizes vary. The UKSOL 460W single panel kit measures 1,762mm x 1,134mm x 30mm and weighs 25.5kg. The 890W kit comprises two panels.
![UKSOL 460W Plug-In Solar Pro kit](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/319347b6767cd04963aae6c28d95971db158707c/31_0_1454_1163/master/1454.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Setting up
The official guidance suggests that it will take about an hour to set up your system. It estimates 15-25% of people will need professional support mounting the panels, and about 15% will need minor electrical works. UKSOL suggests it takes two people to handle and position the panels, as each one weighs 25kg.
Osborne says plug-in solar systems should not be connected via extension leads, cable reels, multiway adaptors, travel adaptors or plug-in RCD adaptors. “These accessories can overheat, become overloaded and create additional safety risks,” he says.
![A man lifts a large solar panel in the garden of a US home](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/87f235d505f0723ceaafcc0a1ac44264c1fd07f3/1059_160_6880_5091/master/6880.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
There is also some other housekeeping. The owner has to tell their distribution network operator that they are using them (there should be a form in the box). You can find out who it is by inputting your postcode on the Energy Networks Association website. You will also be able to consult the ENA’s Connect Direct site for a list of approved devices, which is a good place to start before you buy.
Savings
Plug-in systems are about a fifth of the size of a typical residential rooftop solar system, which means they will not provide enough energy to power a home on their own – but they could cut your bill.
One drawback is that you need to be home to use the power generated because without a battery it is not being stored for later, so flows back to the grid.
However, the adoption of balcony solar could, in time, pave the way for plug-in batteries in British homes, too. If paired with a plug-in solar system, households could store their own renewable electricity during the day and use it to run their appliances in the evenings. The government is reportedly considering plans to bulk-buy the devices and distribute them to low-income homes.
A basic plug-in solar system costs about £400. Parry says it will “give you back, at worst, £40 a year, and at the best about £110. If it’s the worst-case scenario, it’s going to pay for itself in 10 years, but at the best-case scenario, it’s four.
“If you’ve just got 800W, it’s only at its very peak that it will give you that.”
He adds: “The slight downside is that plug-in solar is hitting the markets as the summer’s coming to an end. It’s going to be more use in May next year.”
![A woman adjusts a solar panel on the balcony of a house](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/db305f47d017ab48f3eab7749ec7bd72149787ef/1038_70_5589_4602/master/5589.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Moore says that the level of saving is affected by a number of things, including the system size, location, orientation and actually being home to use the power.
He expects the 460W system his company will be selling to save a typical household about £80-£120 a year, “while the 890W system could save more”.
He adds: “The greatest savings are achieved when households use appliances during daylight hours, as this increases the proportion of generated electricity used within the home.”
You can buy a more expensive 2,000W kit (the inverter will only allow 800W through) to maximise your power-generating capacity, but these are more expensive.
Staying safe
Although there is no obligation to do this, before buying a kit, some experts think you should get your home electrics checked by a professional. That is because this is the first time that British residential wiring circuits will take power in via a three-point socket rather than simply being used to distribute electricity.
Electrical Safety First is concerned about the impact on residual current devices, or RCDs, which sit in a household electricity box and cut off the power if someone drills through a wire or runs their lawnmower over a power cord. Electricians are concerned they may burn out when plug-in solar panels start adding electricity to the circuit.
A Department for Energy Security and Net Zero spokesperson says: “Plug-in solar panels will be available to buy this summer, and stringent verification and registration checks are already in place. They are a transformative technology that can save people hundreds of pounds on their bills.”
Box] Renters
Plug-in solar should make it easier for tenants to take advantage of renewable energy, as any kit they buy can be moved from place to place.
But if you are renting, you should ask permission from your landlord before you invest in any panels.
The rules on what you can do with regard to fixing brackets to hold them, for example, may vary depending on what your tenancy agreement says.
![Couple installing a solar panel outdoors](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/e9f670d45b2769cd79c8d334612b265bd851c1bd/0_0_6830_5464/master/6830.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
There’s “no reason” why your landlord should be against the idea, Parry says. “He or she can look at the information and know it’s super, super safe.”
Meera Chindooroy, the deputy director of campaigns, public affairs and policy at the National Residential Landlords Association, says that while the organisation supports the “principle of tenants benefiting from plug-in solar panels … landlords would first need to be satisfied that the panels meet all required safety standards”.
She adds: “It would not be right for landlords to be held responsible for the safety of equipment they were not asked about in the first place.”
summary: Low-cost "plug-in" solar panels will go on sale in Great Britain following a recent change in wiring regulations allowing systems up to 800 watts to be connected directly to a wall socket without an electrician. These mini solar systems, which can be mounted on balconies, shed roofs, or garden walls, make renewable energy more accessible to renters and those living in flats. While they will not power an entire home on their own, experts estimate they can save households between £40 and £120 annually depending on usage and system size.
key_points: New regulations taking effect on 27 August allow households in Great Britain to connect plug-in solar panels of up to 800 watts directly to a three-prong wall socket.
Major retailers such as B&Q, Currys, Lidl, Wickes, and Amazon plan to sell the kits, with prices starting around £400 to £599.

Experts advise waiting until the regulations take effect, buying from reputable high street retailers rather than third-party marketplace sellers, and notifying the local distribution network operator.
Because the systems do not store power without a battery, households achieve the greatest savings by using appliances during daylight hours while the panels are actively generating electricity.
Renters can use the portable kits but must first seek permission from their landlords and ensure safety standards are met.

title: Unions worry Labour’s plan for zero-hours contracts may break manifesto pledge
author: Heather Stewart
content:
Trades unions are warning Andy Burnham that Labour’s policy on cutting zero-hours contracts risks failing to live up to the party’s manifesto.
Union leaders are seeking reassurances from the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, amid what the TUC has condemned as “scaremongering” from business groups.
The unions were alarmed by limitations on who will qualify for new guaranteed hours contracts, mooted in Labour’s recent consultation document on the policy.
Joanne Thomas, the general secretary of shop workers’ union Usdaw, said: “The right to a contract that guarantees the hours you normally work is a matter of basic fairness and security. It must be applied to everyone to deliver the government’s manifesto commitment.”
She added that the policy “must apply to everyone up to and including full-time workers. We absolutely cannot have loopholes that make this meaningless.”
Ross Holden, the head of policy and research at the GMB union, said: “We are concerned that without a major rethink there is a risk this policy is not matching what we said in the manifesto.”
He added that unions are worried about whether their concerns are being given sufficient weight. “If the policy development is one-sided then we risk this being watered down.”
Unite raised a separate concern, about a “regularity requirement” – suggested by the government – which the union claimed would exclude a significant number of workers.
“If the government was attempting to create a right which virtually no workers could qualify for or be able to enforce – they could not have done a better job,” a Unite spokesperson said.
![a clock with 0s where the hour markers should be](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/ba9ea09bf74052e57240b522c6dbf33fe8925f80/0_0_6256_4175/master/6256.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Getting rid of “exploitative” zero-hours contracts is a key aim of Labour’s Employment Rights Act. The Act has already become law, but the zero hours changes are not due to be implemented until next year, and many details have yet to be thrashed out.
A consultation document, published when Keir Starmer was still at No 10, included an upper hours threshold. Workers whose existing contract already guarantees them more than the threshold – which could be set at anything from 8 to 48 hours – would not qualify for the new right to a contract that matches the hours they actually work.
Business groups seized on official estimates published by the government last week that showed the most expansive version of the policy could cost companies up to £2.9bn a year. The British Chambers of Commerce called the prospect “a further hammer blow for many firms struggling to keep their heads above water”.
Kate Bell, the assistant general secretary of the TUC, said that 40% of the upper costs estimate was made up of the compensation employers would have to pay out for cancelling workers’ shifts at short notice. “That assumes no behavioural change by employers,” she said. “It assumes they don’t have the creativity and the experience to adapt their model.”
after newsletter promotion
Bell added that the same document showed irregular and unpredictable shifts cost one in three workers on zero-hours contracts about £3,000 a year.
“We keep having to have the same argument time and time again about the real costs of insecurity for workers,” she said. “Most people don’t want to be on these contracts. They’ve been on these contracts for a long time and it has costs for their mental health and their financial security.”
Reynolds returned to the job of business secretary in Burnham’s wholesale reshuffle last month, after being moved out of the post by Starmer. With the zero hours consultation closing next week, the issue will be one of the first he faces back in post.
A government spokesperson said: “We are absolutely committed to ending exploitative zero-hours contracts, where workers bear all the financial risk when hours, shifts and earnings are unpredictable. These reforms will give workers in every postcode greater income security and predictability of hours.”
The spokesperson added: “While no final decisions have been made, we’re consulting with business and trade unions including GMB, Unite and Usdaw, to get the detail right and ensure this works in the real world.”
summary: Trades unions are warning that Labour's proposed policy on zero-hours contracts risks failing to meet manifesto commitments due to potential limitations and loopholes. Union leaders are seeking reassurances from Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds as the consultation period nears its close. The concerns center around proposed qualifications, such as upper hours thresholds and regularity requirements, which unions fear will exclude many workers.
key_points: Union leaders warn that Labour's zero-hours contract plans may break manifesto pledges by excluding certain workers through policy loopholes.
Unions including Usdaw, GMB, and Unite have raised alarms over proposed restrictions like upper hours thresholds and regularity requirements.
Business groups have warned of high potential costs for companies, while the TUC argues those estimates assume no behavioral change by employers.
The government stated that no final decisions have been made and that it is consulting with both businesses and trade unions to finalize the details.

title: Houses on Anglesey estate cannot be sold as family homes
author: Danielle Herbert
content:
![Four semi-detached modern homes at the end of a street. There are solar panels on the roof and wooden cladding on the top of the buildings. Each home is painted a different colour. They are grown, green, yellow and grey.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/c3e5/live/6a091240-9def-11f1-898b-91bf436c749f.jpg)
At least 37 families have asked about buying the properties as homes
- Published
An almost empty new build estate has sparked anger because rules state that the houses can be only sold as holiday homes, with one would-be buyer saying her grandparents would be "turning in their graves".
Parc Delfryn, Brynteg, is two miles from the Anglesey coast and home to the second highest rate of holiday home users, external in Wales for its population size, yet 14 of the 16 houses have not been sold since 2023.
But planning restrictions imposed before construction began mean they cannot be sold to people who want to live there and a challenge to the rules failed.
Anglesey council said changing rules would "set a dangerous precedent" for holiday homes approved around the island.
"What I can't get my head around is that the council think this is right for the area," said Jane Roberts, who grew up in Brynteg.
"They do not realise the impact it's having on local people."
She had plans to move back to the area, where her family have lived for generations, in 2024.
But realised if she wanted to buy one of these homes, she would have to rent out her home in Llangefni to do so.
Since April 2024, second home owners on Anglesey pay an extra 100% council tax on their properties - unless the property is let out for at least 182 days a year.
This followed a Wales-wide plan to allow councils to charge up to four times their current level of council tax as part of efforts to make it easier for people to afford homes where they grew up.
In June 2023, the BBC reported Anglesey had seen the biggest jump in holiday home users in England and Wales over the past 10 years.
As of late 2023, some 10% of the island's housing stock was classed as either second or holiday homes, according to planning documents - higher than in other areas of Wales and in the UK.
![Jane Roberts has blonde shoulder length hair. She is photographed outside in a garden. She is smiling and looking at the camera.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/549/cpsprodpb/540b/live/9cd20470-9def-11f1-898b-91bf436c749f.jpg)
Jane Roberts has fond memories of growing up in Brynteg, where her father and grandparents were born
"I didn't feel right about it," she said.
"My father and grandparents would turn in their graves if they saw these houses could not be sold to local buyers.
"It has put me off looking at other properties in the village."
One estate agent said there had been no viewings on the estate for 18 months.
Roberts, 66, said Brynteg, where her father and grandparents were born, "was a lovely village to grow up in".
"We had the best childhood growing up there."
She said her daughter, who lives in Brynteg with her children, was "not happy about this situation at all", like "a lot of people" living there.
"It's not a good look for the area. It doesn't create a good feeling," she added.
![A man with grey hair, stood outside in a car park. He is looking directly at the camera. He is wearing a dark grey knitted quarter zip jumper, with a high neck.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/dd6f/live/af9f6700-9def-11f1-898b-91bf436c749f.jpg)
Phil Morrill says the homes are "no use to anyone just lying empty"
Roberts is not the only person from Brynteg who has struggled to understand the council's decision.
"There's too much red tape... it's terrible, it really is," said Phil Morrill.
"There should be nothing to stop anyone from buying and living in these... it doesn't make any sense at all. They're no use to anyone just lying empty like that."
"It doesn't make any sense that local people shouldn't be able to buy and live in these houses," said Richard Jones.
"It's a good spot, right near a village pub, they would be ideal as family homes.
"It would be even better if the council bought them as social housing and rented them out, seeing as they're empty."
![Richard Jones is stood in front of a large grassy field. He has short grey hair and is smiling and looking at the camera.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/838f/live/bf36f2f0-9def-11f1-898b-91bf436c749f.jpg)
Richard Jones said "it doesn't make any sense" that locals are unable to buy the empty properties
Mike Williams of Beresford Adams is one of two estate agents trying to sell the holiday homes, and said leaving "perfectly good properties" empty was a "complete and utter waste of money".
Williams, who lives in Brynteg, said he was "frustrated" that homes "perfect" for local people have been "left lying dormant".
"We've literally had no viewings on the development for about a year-and-a-half," he added.
"The second home market was never really interested in places like Brynteg, they were more interested in places like Benllech and Moelfre, which are closer to the coast."
![Mike Williams is photographed standing in front of a map of Anglesey. He has short grey hair and is wearing a black shirt.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/b771/live/cf0e4700-9def-11f1-898b-91bf436c749f.jpg)
Estate agent Mike Williams says homes "perfect" for local people have been "left lying dormant"
In a planning report, external, PLanD development consultants said at least 37 families, the majority local to Anglesey, had asked about buying the properties as homes in the "tight-knit community".
Williams said people living in Brynteg and nearby knew the homes were empty and cannot be sold for residential use, leading to no further inquiries about them.
PLanD planning consultant Simon James said the council tax changes for second homes in Wales had "killed the holiday home market".
"These houses are built, they're sat there, and they are being left idle," he added.
He believes a change of use for the properties would be "beneficial" and help meet housing needs in the area.
PLanD confirmed it would appeal against the decision by the council to refuse the change of use to residential properties.
![two semi-detached modern homes with solar panels on the roof. There is wooden cladding on the top of the buildings. A blue for sale sign can be seen outside the front of the properties.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/2310/live/ef567000-9def-11f1-898b-91bf436c749f.jpg)
Out of the 16 properties, only two have been bought since construction was finished almost three years ago
In a statement, the council acknowledged comments made by local residents, but said to support the application to make the homes available to buy on the open market, the applicant "needed to provide evidence that the approved holiday accommodation scheme was no longer financially viable".
It said a "detailed" viability assessment and supporting information had been requested "on a number of occasions" but was not provided - without which it could not support the application.
It added: "Approving the proposal without the necessary supporting information would have gone against the planning policy framework and could have set a precedent for similar applications elsewhere on the island."

summary: An almost empty new build estate at Parc Delfryn in Brynteg, Anglesey, has sparked local anger because planning restrictions mean the homes can only be sold as holiday accommodations. Since completion in 2023, 14 of the 16 properties have remained unsold, with estate agents reporting no viewings in 18 months due to a weakened holiday home market and high local demand. Anglesey council rejected a challenge to change the rules, stating the applicant failed to provide necessary financial viability evidence and that approval without it would set a dangerous precedent.
key_points: At Parc Delfryn in Brynteg, 14 out of 16 newly built homes have remained unsold since 2023 due to planning restrictions limiting them to holiday use.
At least 37 families, mostly local, have inquired about purchasing the properties as permanent family homes.
Anglesey council defended its decision, stating the applicant failed to provide a requested financial viability assessment to support changing the rules.
Experts note that recent council tax increases for second homes in Wales have negatively impacted the holiday home market.

title: Britain turns to floating wind farms as it runs out of shallow waters
author: Jonathan Leake
content:
![Floating offshore wind turbines](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/20/TELEMMGLPICT000498937050_17872329442940_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqRo0U4xU-30oDveS4pXV-Vv4Xpit_DMGvdp2n7FDd82k.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Floating offshore wind turbines](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/20/TELEMMGLPICT000498937050_17872329442940_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqRo0U4xU-30oDveS4pXV-Vv4Xpit_DMGvdp2n7FDd82k.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
It could be Ed Miliband’s most expensive legacy. A network of giant floating wind farms is set to fill Britain’s seas – funded by some of the most generous green subsidies ever offered.
Just before Andy Burnham shunted him over to the Foreign Office, the former energy secretary signed off plans for hundreds of floating turbines to be moored around Scotland, Wales and Cornwall.
Such waters are too deep for wind turbines that are drilled directly into the seabed and floating versions have always been too expensive for companies to bother.
So Miliband approved a raft of generous new subsidies targeted at making floating wind profitable – guaranteeing generators prices three to four times above current market value for up to 20 years.
“Floating offshore wind is at the heart of the Government’s mission to make Britain a clean energy superpower,” he said when first announcing the plan.
“By leading the world in this cutting-edge technology, we can speed up the transition to home-grown clean energy, increasing our energy security and creating good jobs.”
What it means in practice is that he and Miatta Fahnbulleh, the new Energy Secretary, want to see an estimated 3,000 or so new floating turbines anchored around UK coasts in the next 10 to 15 years – with about 500 in place by 2030 alone.
The machines would add 30 gigawatts (GW) of generating capacity, fed back to the mainland by thousands of miles of subsea electrical cables, connected to the grid via a network of new onshore substations.
Later this autumn, the bill for those plans will begin to come clear when the results of the latest “allocation round” are published. This is the process in which the Government offers guaranteed minimum prices for low-carbon generation.
Floating wind farms have been offered about £270 per megawatt hour (MWh) – about three to four times the normal price of wholesale electricity.
When those farms start operating, those extra costs will cascade on to our energy bills – already among the world’s highest.
So why then is the Government so keen to build yet more wind farms – at premium prices?
Supporters argue that floating wind is the obvious next step in Britain’s pivot away from fossil fuels.
We have already filled our shallower seas under 60 metres deep with fixed turbines.
Floating technology would open up vast tracts of deeper ocean including the waters around most of Scotland, the Irish Sea and the Celtic Sea off Cornwall.
Supporters argue that the technology will become much cheaper as it matures – as has already happened with fixed offshore wind, solar and other renewables.
Opponents disagree. They say the UK has already added billions of pounds to energy bills through subsidies to offshore and onshore wind, solar and nuclear generation – and floating wind just adds more to that burden.
Some even challenge the need for floating wind, pointing out that UK electricity consumption has fallen by 20pc in the last two decades.
Despite the questions, floating wind has been a fixture of UK energy generation for some time.
Floating off Scotland’s east coast are the predecessors of what Labour hopes will be Britain’s next renewable energy revolution.
The five turbines in the Hywind floating wind farm off Peterhead have been generating power since 2017.
Anchored in water up to 120m deep, they have routinely outperformed fixed offshore turbines, achieving around 54pc capacity because winds tend to be stronger over deeper offshore waters.
Just down the coast lies the UK’s other floating wind farm, the Kincardine offshore site.
Technically both have been a success – but at a high price.
Hywind and Kincardine were funded under an older subsidy system which guaranteed them up to £230 per MWh plus the price of the electricity – again, three to four times the cost of wholesale power.
The hit to our bills has so far been tiny because Hywind and Kincardine are small test-beds for an emerging technology.
Floating wind is, however, set to get very big indeed.
Trade body Renewable UK’s tracking of new projects shows another nine floating wind farms already have planning permission with another eight seeking consent and 25 more in development.
Collectively, they will add another 30 GW or so to UK generating capacity – equivalent to all the wind farms Britain has built to date.
Luke Clark, from Renewable UK, says Britain could become a world leader in floating wind if it acts now.
“Designing and manufacturing foundations for floating wind farms could add over £10bn to our economy over a 10-year period,” he says. “By 2050, the UK’s floating wind industry could employ 97,000 people, contributing £47bn to our economy.”
Analysts challenge the real value for money.
Dr John Constable, the director of the Renewable Energy Foundation, said: “Floating offshore wind has to overcome the low power density of wind in a truly savage marine environment and high costs are inevitable ... so it will remain expensive even compared to conventional offshore wind.
“None of this appears to be good value for the consumer.”
![Floating wind turbine](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/20/TELEMMGLPICT000498935109_17872328896730_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bq7HVybmJHsiZ-in9phuBAJ0ikPYR0xYwuEBLwP9UFqPg.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
The potential scale of the project is, however, huge.
There are plans for 260 floating wind turbines between the coasts of South Wales and North Cornwall – held in place by 1,000 massive anchors – and more than 500km of cable criss-crossing the seabed.
Users of Britain’s deep seas, including oil and gas companies, cargo vessels, leisure sailors and fishing vessels also risk being displaced by floating wind farms.
The potential disruption goes much further than the actual wind farms.
The turbines will have to be constructed, stored and serviced close to shore in designated areas.
These will feature dozens of giant buoys anchored with massive chains, where components, often built overseas, will be brought to the UK and assembled into turbines before being towed out to windfarm sites.
The first of these parks, planned for the Moray Firth, will be around 35 sq km in size, with others planned around Scotland and in the Celtic Sea.
It means seaside villages, recreational sailors and inshore fishermen will see once pristine seascapes dominated by heavy industry and vessel traffic.
Mike Cohen, the chief executive of the National Federation of Fishermen’s Organisations, says: “The unique feature of floating turbines is how they anchor to the seabed.
“With around 80 turbines in each array, the sites will be criss-crossed with an underwater web of massive cables, hanging in mid-water. It will be impossible for fishing boats to operate.”
Elspeth Macdonald, the chief executive of the Scottish Fishermen’s Federation, says fishing vessels would be excluded from floating wind farms.
She says: “Floating wind farms have moorings, cables and associated infrastructure that make co-existence with most fishing practically impossible.
“We recognise the need for renewable energy, but the seas underpin the country’s food security.”
Such arguments are unlikely to cut much ice with Labour, which is firmly locked into supporting floating wind.
It has offered UK port owners a £160m capital grant scheme to upgrade harbours with the deep-water quays and heavy lifting gear needed for such giant structures.
A Department for Energy Security and Net Zero spokesman said: “The industry will build on expertise from sectors such as oil and gas to create jobs, attract investment and strengthen Britain’s energy security.”
summary: Britain is turning to floating offshore wind farms as shallow waters become fully utilized, with plans to install roughly 3,000 new turbines over the next 10 to 15 years. To make the technology profitable, the government has approved generous subsidies guaranteeing prices three to four times higher than current market value, which critics warn will drive up consumer energy bills. While supporters argue the initiative will enhance energy security and create jobs, opponents and fishing industry representatives raise concerns over high costs, heavy industry dominating coastal areas, and the displacement of fishing vessels.
key_points: Britain's government has signed off on plans for hundreds of floating wind turbines to be moored around Scotland, Wales, and Cornwall because shallow waters are already filled with fixed turbines.

Floating wind farms have been offered guaranteed prices of about £270 per megawatt hour, which is three to four times the normal wholesale electricity price and will add extra costs to consumer energy bills.

Supporters believe the technology will boost energy security, add billions to the economy, and create thousands of jobs, while existing test-bed sites like Hywind and Kincardine have successfully generated power since 2017.
Critics and fishing industry leaders warn that the massive anchors, cables, and infrastructure will make co-existence impossible for fishing boats and ruin pristine seascapes with heavy industry.

title: FX Daily: Much ado about buybacks, softer dollar
source: ING THINK economic and financial analysis | ING THINK
author: Chris Turner; Francesco Pesole; Frantisek Taborsky
content:
This week's US Treasury intervention in the bond market has caused much furore amongst the buy and sell-side financial community alike. We see the move more as a signalling tool that the US Treasury has a problem with high bond yields and wants to address it. For the time being, we favour this triggering a benign, risk-friendly dollar decline
![Most paths lead to a weaker dollar; we prefer the pro-risk route](https://think.ing.com/uploads/hero/_webp/w568h320_shutterstock_1353591350_.jpg_webp_40cd750bba9870f18aada2478b24840a.webp) 
USD: Most paths favour a softer dollar
Many commentators seem to be treating this week's US Treasury intervention in bond markets as a heinous financial crime. We prefer to take the view offered by a former US Treasury official interviewed in the Financial Times today that this was a signalling exercise. Yes, these buy-back operations were originally designed to address market liquidity issues and the off-cycle nature of the adjustment has raised eyebrows. But the main takeaway has to be that higher longer-dated Treasury yields are firmly on the Treasury's radar and need to be addressed. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent suggested yesterday that there might be some new fiscal consolidation plans incoming. These could centre on a task force to cut back on fraud in the same way that Elon Musk's DOGE tried to cut back on government spending. Most are sceptical that this will make any dent in the near 6% budget deficit, but let's see what is announced.
For the dollar, quite a few are comparing this week's Treasury buybacks to President Donald Trump's 'Liberation Day' tariffs and concluding this again undermines US policy credibility. During that period in April 2025, the Swiss franc, the euro and the yen led the charge against a weaker dollar. We see this week's developments less as a policy credibility story and more as a soft dollar, pro-risk story if the US Treasury is taking a greater interest in protecting the long end. That probably means a gentler dollar decline and some outperformance of high-beta commodity currencies and emerging market currencies in general. If we're wrong and Treasuries and equities start selling off hard, then the story would revert to a lower USD/CHF, higher EUR/USD and high-yield FX selling off as volatility rises.
On today's US calendar are the S&P PMI readings for August – all expecting continued expansion in activity.
DXY has support in this 98.65/70 region and will probably struggle to make it back above 99.00 now.
Chris Turner
EUR: US fiscal consolidation would be EUR/USD positive
EUR/USD remains well supported, and, as above, we favour the kind of benign decline in the dollar that tends to float all boats. Not that anyone is expecting it, but should some true US fiscal consolidation emerge, the combination of tighter fiscal policy and looser monetary policy would be dollar-negative. Fiscal consolidation seems unlikely though, with Washington wanting to spread its pro-growth mindset to the entire G20 when finance ministers and central bank governors meet later this month.
Today's eurozone data calendar focuses on the August PMIs. For the eurozone as a whole, these are expected to indicate a continued mild expansion and one which supports another European Central Bank hike in September. There will also be focus on the ECB's Consumer Expectations Survey, where three-year inflation expectations reached 3.0% in March and are expected to remain elevated at 2.8%.
With emerging market currencies performing well, we prefer a continued gentle rise in EUR/USD. High natural gas prices remain a concern, but since the eurozone economy seems to be coping with these better now, EUR/USD can focus on the soft dollar story.
EUR/USD can consolidate in a tight 1.1670-1.1710 range today, before potentially edging higher.
Chris Turner
CHF: This is not April 2025
Wednesday's US Treasury announcement on buy-backs saw USD/CHF lead the dollar lower. This recalled events of April 2025, when concerns over policy credibility hit all US classes and the dollar, while the Swiss franc was preferred. Our take on this week's events is different. We think the sharp sell-off in USD/CHF was driven by position adjustment after the June narrative of a more hawkish Fed had favoured USD/CHF longs.
If we're right that greater interest in protecting the Treasury market is more a risk-positive story, then volatility will stay low, and interest will remain firm in the carry trade. Here, we think the Swiss franc rather than the yen will increasingly become the preferred funding currency and send EUR/CHF back to 0.9400. We are encouraged by the EUR/CHF bounce back above 0.9350 since Wednesday.
Chris Turner
ZAR: External environment helps rand
Our softer dollar, pro-risk environment favours high-yielding commodity currencies like the rand. The rand normally has a decent correlation with the Chinese renminbi, which is performing quite well along with large parts of Asian FX. We can see USD/ZAR pressing the April low at 15.92 and then perhaps testing the 15.75/80 area. One area of concern for the rand later this year, however, could be El Niño, where drought conditions could cause some major problems.
Chris Turner

Analysts suggest this move supports a benign, risk-friendly dollar decline, benefiting high-beta commodity currencies and emerging market assets. Meanwhile, upcoming data releases include US and eurozone August S&P PMI readings and the ECB's Consumer Expectations Survey.

The intervention is expected to foster a benign and risk-friendly dollar decline rather than severely undermine policy credibility.
US fiscal consolidation plans may be incoming, though skepticism remains regarding their impact on the budget deficit.
High-yielding commodity currencies like the South African rand are positioned to benefit from the softer dollar and positive external environment.

title: More than 10 million people face hosepipe ban until end of year, water supplier says
author: Dan Haygarth
content:
Thames Water has said its hosepipe ban is likely to be enforced until the end of the year.
More than 27 million people across England have now had hosepipe use restricted in their area, including Thames Water’s 10.1 million customers after a ban was put in place last month.
After several heatwaves over a record-breaking summer and historic lows of rainfall, hosepipe restrictions in England’s capital and surrounding areas could last for several months, the water firm said.
Nevil Muncaster, strategic water resources director at Thames Water, told Times Radio: “I think realistically, it’s going to be towards the end of the year before that comes off.
“That’s something that we need to make sure we do just to protect the environment.”
Earlier this week, it urged customers to continue efforts to reduce water use as it revealed household demand has fallen by 3 per cent across London and more than 6 per cent across the Thames Valley and Home Counties since a hosepipe ban began on 23 July.
In an update on Tuesday, the utility said London reservoir storage was at 74 per cent, which is lower than what the firm would expect for this time of year but the Farmoor Reservoir in Oxfordshire is 92 per cent full.
It also said rainfall in the Thames catchment area during July was less than 1mm, which is just 2 per cent of the long-term average, while customers used around 100 million litres more water every day than normal, adding further pressure to rivers, reservoirs and the water network.
Mr Muncaster said that dry conditions were still expected, even though some rain is forecast to fall.
“The Environment Agency forecast is that it will be drier than normal for the next few months, but we’ll wait and see,” he added.
The beleaguered water firm, which is the country’s largest, is struggling under almost £20bn in debt, with cash running out to see the firm through beyond the end of this year and widespread concern about which direction is best for the future of the business.
Mr Muncaster told Times Radio that a new reservoir at Abingdon in Oxfordshire is unlikely to be ready until 2040.
He also defended the fact that the company’s £250m Beckton desalination plant, which opened in 2010 to provide water during droughts, had been offline this summer.
He said: “It was something we planned. We had a very wet winter, so we took the opportunity to do that maintenance, expecting us to be able to work through the summer.”
summary: Thames Water announced that its current hosepipe ban affecting over 10 million customers will likely remain in place until the end of the year to protect the environment. The restrictions follow a record-breaking summer with historic lows in rainfall and multiple heatwaves that severely strained water resources and reservoir levels. Despite some upcoming rain forecasts, dry conditions are expected to persist over the next few months.
key_points: Over 10 million Thames Water customers face hosepipe restrictions likely lasting until the end of the year.
The ban was implemented following extreme summer heatwaves and historic lows in rainfall, with July seeing less than 1mm of rain in the Thames catchment area.
Household water demand has fallen since the ban began on 23 July, dropping by 3 per cent in London and over 6 per cent in the Thames Valley and Home Counties.
Thames Water's Beckton desalination plant remained offline this summer due to planned maintenance following a wet winter.
A proposed new reservoir at Abingdon in Oxfordshire is not expected to be ready until 2040.

title: Ready for plug-in solar panels? UKSOL announces regulatory compliance with ground mount kits going on sale in a week from £699
author: Darren Allan
content:
![A UKSOL plug-in solar kit](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/zhFxW4ku7LCEqbPaAWYpJa.jpg) 
- UKSOL says it's the first in the UK to achieve regulatory compliance for plug-in solar products
- It's ground mount kits with one or two solar panels go on sale on August 27
- That's when solar is legal in the UK, and we can expect more of these kits to be available
UKSOL has announced that it's the first solar company in the UK to achieve regulatory compliance for plug-in solar kits, the first of which will be on sale in just a week.
Those products are the UKSOL Plug-In Solar Pro Compact 460W Ground Mount Kit (consisting of a single solar panel), and the Plug-In Solar Pro Duo 890W Ground Mount Kit (two panels). Both of these go on sale from August 27 in the UK — when plug-in kits become legal in this country — albeit in "limited stocks" to begin with.
A pair of hybrid mount kits — a single panel 515W offering, and a 920W two-panel product — have also been approved, and these should be available in October 2026 (or that's the current plan).
All of these have met the relevant regulatory standards, and are listed as 'compliant' in the ENA (Energy Network Association) Connect Direct plug-in solar device database.
The Plug-In Solar Pro products have been developed specifically for the British market, UKSOL informs us in a press release, and these are all-in-one kits that come with everything you need to be up and running.
With the kits out next week, alongside the UKSOL panel(s) you get an integrated (foldable) ground-mounting frame with a ballast tray, as well as the necessary 800W microinverter plus DC and AC cables. There's a smartphone app for monitoring the system, too.
Pricing for the Pro Compact (single panel) 460W Ground Mount Kit is £849 with VAT and two-man delivery included, with the Pro Duo 890W Ground Mount Kit running to £1,199 (also with VAT and delivery). The RRP at retailers is £699 and £1,089 respectively.

Andrew Moore, the CEO of UKSOL, commented: "We expect plug in solar to become an exciting new consumer category, but there is a real responsibility on manufacturers and retailers to get the introduction right. Consumers should be able to understand who manufactured or supplied their system, what testing has been undertaken, what warranty and technical support sits behind it and whether it meets the requirements for the UK market."
He added: "Price will obviously matter, but solar equipment is a long-term electrical product. Safety, provenance, quality and after-sales support need to matter too."
Analysis: An alternative to full solar is (almost) here
 ![A UKSOL plug-in solar kit](https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/tUcfCFcevsjbUD2kzwnXPa.jpg) 
The ground mount kits are, of course, placed on the ground in your garden or other outside area (and weighed down using the ballast tray, to ensure that if it gets windy, you aren't going to end up with overturned panels).
The other option from UKSOL is to buy a hybrid mount kit in October, and these can be situated on the ground, or on a wall (or balcony). They'll arrive in a 515W compact (one panel) variant and an 890W dual panel setup, with other offerings too (up to a 1260W hybrid kit). No pricing is available for those yet.
Kits from other manufacturers should be going on sale soon enough as plug-in solar becomes legal on August 27, when UKSOL's first ground mount offerings become available. Manufacturers must ensure compliance with UK regulations, of course, as UKSOL has done, with the likes of Asda, Currys, B&Q, Wickes, and Screwfix potentially stocking these solutions.
Plug-in panels offer a good alternative as a scaled-down version of a full roof-mounted solar setup, as not every house can have the latter — flats certainly can't, and some roofs just aren't suitable. Plug-in solar is the obvious choice if you're renting, and don't own the property, too — and they're a lot less of a financial commitment than a full roof installation.
A typical payback period for plug-in (when the electricity saved roughly equals the cost of the panels) is three to five years, according to the experts, which is way quicker than a typical full solar install.
Note that there are certain requirements in terms of the rules for the location of plug-in solar panels — you can't put them on wooden balconies for example (due to the fire risk), and the same goes for fences.

The all-in-one kits, including single and dual-panel options with microinverters and mounting frames, coincide with plug-in solar becoming legal in the UK. Additional hybrid mount kits that can be placed on the ground, walls, or balconies are planned for release in October 2026.

The initial 460W single-panel and 890W two-panel ground mount kits launch on August 27, priced from £699 RRP.

title: Fashion tech founder sentenced to prison for $300m fraud scheme
author: Victoria Bekiempis
content:
A fashion tech founder was sentenced to five years in federal prison for her involvement in a $300m “fraud scheme” spanning from 2019 to 2025, the Manhattan US attorney’s office announced on Thursday. Christine Hunsicker, 49, was also sentenced to three years of supervised release.
Hunsicker, the founder and ex-CEO of CaaStle Inc, had pleaded guilty this March to one count of securities fraud in relation to a scheme that “defrauded hundreds of investors”, authorities said. Her attorneys did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Hunsicker, a “well-known entrepreneur and businessperson in the fashion-tech industry”, touted CaaStle as a fast-growing business with a valuation of more than $1.4bn, the southern district of New York prosecutor’s office said. But Hunsicker knew that the company was reeling “in financial distress with dwindling cash and significant expenses”.
Hunsicker gave investors a slew of phoney documents to raise money for CaaStle, such as “falsified income statements, fake audited financial statements, fictitious bank records, and sham corporate documents” that dramatically exaggerated the company’s profits and cash reserves. Although Hunsicker told investors that their money would be directed toward buying discounted shares from then-shareholders, prosecutors said she “fabricated the existence of these shareholders”.
Then, prosecutors said, Hunsicker used this money as new capital for the company while hiding CaaStle’s financial situation. Federal authorities allege that Hunsicker continued engaging in fraudulent behavior “even after law enforcement agents seized her electronic devices in March 2025”.
CaaStle went bankrupt after the company revealed in spring 2025 that Hunsicker had significantly exaggerated the company’s finances, according to the New York Times. The company reportedly began as a web-based clothing rental company for plus-sized women and ultimately started selling its platform to outside fashion companies.
summary: Christine Hunsicker, the 49-year-old founder and ex-CEO of CaaStle Inc, was sentenced to five years in federal prison for orchestrating a $300m fraud scheme. She pleaded guilty to securities fraud after using falsified documents to deceive investors about the company's financial health and valuation. Despite the company's severe financial distress and ultimate bankruptcy in 2025, Hunsicker continued her fraudulent activities even after law enforcement seized her electronic devices.
key_points: Christine Hunsicker was sentenced to five years in federal prison and three years of supervised release.
She pleaded guilty to one count of securities fraud related to a $300m investor fraud scheme spanning from 2019 to 2025.
Hunsicker provided investors with fake financial records, falsified income statements, and sham corporate documents to exaggerate CaaStle's profits and cash reserves.
Prosecutors stated that Hunsicker continued engaging in fraud even after federal authorities seized her electronic devices in March 2025.
CaaStle filed for bankruptcy after disclosing in the spring of 2025 that Hunsicker had significantly exaggerated the company's financial standing.

title: UK posts unexpected budget deficit in July as spending rises
author: Andy Bruce
content:
UK posts unexpected budget deficit in July as spending rises
![](https://s.yimg.com/lo/mysterio/api/B656A7C7BA0A78BAD7DEA4EA838940D6C5F97AE32F997DA25384D002A5311417/subgraphmysterio/resizefit_w960_h640;quality_80;format_webp/https:%2F%2Fmedia.zenfs.com%2Fen%2Freuters.com%2F454b555b4cdce90fbb3e0ad7b9cbf338.jpg)
By Andy Bruce
MANCHESTER, England, Aug 21 (Reuters) - Britain's government recorded an unexpected budget deficit last month, a reminder of the financial constraints facing new finance minister John Healey ahead of his October budget in spite of recent better news on the economy.
The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said public sector net borrowing was £1.8 billion ($2.5 billion) in July, as higher government spending caused by inflation counteracted record self-assessed income tax receipts for the month.
A Reuters poll of economists had pointed to a balanced budget, while the Office for Budget Responsibility's (OBR) projections had pencilled in a £500 million surplus — which would have been the first for any July since before the COVID-19 pandemic.
But the ONS said central government expenditure on social benefits was up £2 billion in July compared with a year ago, while spending on goods and services — which includes staff costs — was up £1.2 billion.
The deficit for June was revised down sharply to £12.8 billion from £16.0 billion. Still, borrowing for the first four months of the 2026/27 financial year remains higher than the OBR's forecast, at £56.7 billion versus £54.4 billion.
"We expect government borrowing to exceed the OBR forecast over the rest of the year as spending continues to rise," said Thomas Pugh, chief economist at tax and consulting firm RSM.
"Higher gilt yields, stubborn inflation, and a government determined to spend more means borrowing is on course to remain above 4% of GDP this year, instead of falling to 3.6% as projected."
The current budget deficit, which measures day-to-day spending against tax revenues and must be balanced in 2029/30 according to the current fiscal rules, stood at £34.7 billion over the April-July period, against the OBR's projection of £36.7 billion.
"Fiscal discipline is the bedrock of our UK economic stability and national security which is why we are committed to meeting our fiscal rules, with a buffer against global uncertainties," Healey said in a statement.
Future revisions to the data could help Healey. The ONS has revised down its estimates for public sector net borrowing compared with the initial reading in every month this calendar year.
Borrowing in May and June has been revised down by £7.5 billion combined.
The debt interest bill was £700 million higher than a year ago. An ONS statistician said he expected this to rise sharply when data are released for September, reflecting inflation trends and the timing of interest payments on bonds.
($1 = 0.7324 pounds)
(Reporting by Andy Bruce; Editing by William James and Emelia Sithole-Matarise)
summary: Britain's government recorded an unexpected budget deficit of £1.8 billion in July as rising inflation-driven spending offset record income tax receipts. Economists had polled for a balanced budget, while projections had previously anticipated a surplus. The data highlights ongoing financial constraints for finance minister John Healey ahead of the October budget.
key_points: Public sector net borrowing reached £1.8 billion in July.
A Reuters poll of economists had pointed to a balanced budget, while the OBR projected a £500 million surplus.
Central government expenditure increased, driven by a £2 billion rise in social benefit spending and a £1.2 billion increase in goods and services spending.
Borrowing for the first four months of the financial year stands at £56.7 billion, exceeding the OBR's forecast of £54.4 billion.
Finance minister John Healey stated a commitment to meeting fiscal rules and maintaining economic stability.

title: Gold And Silver Hit Highest Prices In Months—Here’s Why
author: Conor Murray
content:
Topline
Precious metals prices are finally rallying after a mostly stagnant summer, with gold hitting its highest price in three months on Friday and silver hitting its highest level in two months, which analysts are largely attributing to a weaker dollar and the Treasury Department’s announcement it would ramp up buybacks of longer-dated government debt.
Key Facts
Gold futures hit their highest level since about mid-May on Friday, rising about 2% to reach a price of $4,661.70.
Silver rose a similar amount, inching up about 2% to hit a price of $70.08, marking the first time the precious metal has crossed the $70 threshold since about mid-June.
Both metals are ending this week about 5% higher, marking a price rally that follows a mostly stagnant summer in which their prices did not budge much.
Ole S. Hansen, an analyst at Saxo Bank, posted on X Friday a softer dollar is one of the key drivers of commodity prices rising, as the dollar index is down very slightly Friday morning—about 0.02%—but is hovering around a three-month low.
UBS Group AG chief strategist Bhanu Baweja also told Bloomberg the rise in metals prices is partially because of the Treasury Department’s announcement it would double buybacks of 10-to-30 year securities, calling the move “a very important signal for gold.”
How Are Gold And Silver Prices Faring This Summer?
Gold and silver have largely come down from the historic highs they reached earlier this year, as gold languished between roughly $4,000 and $4,200 and silver hovered between $50 and $60 for much of the summer. For the quarter ending June 30, gold shed 16% of its value, representing its worst quarter in more than a decade. Around that time, gold and silver had fallen to seven-month lows, erasing some of the gains the metals made during a historic price rally that ended in January of this year. Analysts blamed the summer slump on factors including a then-stronger dollar and expectations that the Federal Reserve may raise interest rates at some point this year. Gold and silver have started to surge again in August, though, as gold recorded its best week in seven months earlier this month.
Will The Federal Reserve Raise Interest Rates This Year?
It’s possible the Fed could raise interest rates later this year, a move that typically depresses gold and silver prices. CME Group’s FedWatch tool says the probability of a rate hike at the Fed’s December meeting is about 70.9%, much higher than the likelihood of a rate increase at the central bank’s September or October meetings.
key background
Gold and silver rose to historic highs earlier this year, with gold topping off around $5,600 and silver reaching about $121 in late January. Prices were buoyed by factors including international tensions, President Donald Trump’s tariffs, interest rate cuts and increasing demand for metals from technological sectors. Prices fell in January after Trump named Kevin Warsh as his choice to lead the Federal Reserve, as Warsh was viewed as less likely to cut rates. Metals prices largely declined throughout the Iran war, as metals generally traded inversely with oil prices, which spiked.
